title: Bread with a side of smoke
hook: Bakers sell exactly what buyers want. Who pays for the smoke?

knows: that a market price balances what buyers will pay with what sellers must receive
doesNotKnow: that when a cost falls on others the market makes more than the true cost justifies

misconception: The market quantity is the best quantity.
objective: The learner can explain that a cost left out of the price makes the market quantity too high: with $1 of smoke per loaf in the model, the true-cost quantity is 35 loaves, not 40.

claims.text: In the model (buyers' price (100 - q) / 10, bakers' cost (q + 20) / 10), the market makes 40 loaves, at a price of $6.
claims.source: (100 - q) / 10 = (q + 20) / 10 gives q = 40; price = 6.00. Demo.tsx MARKET.

claims.text: With $1 of smoke harm per loaf added to the bakers' cost, the buyers' price equals the true cost at 35 loaves.
Loaves 36 to 40 are worth less to buyers than they truly cost (bakers' cost plus $1 of smoke); the stage shades that wedge between the buyers' line and the true-cost line.
claims.source: At q=36 buyers 6.4 vs true cost 6.6; at q=40 buyers 6.00 vs 7.00 (node; Demo.tsx buyers(), bakers()).

claims.text: In the model, a $1 per-loaf cost put on the bakers moves the market quantity to 35 loaves; the stage labels it 'bakers + $1 cost'.
A cost that falls on others is left out of the price, so more is made than the true cost justifies.
claims.source: Textbook definition of a negative externality (e.g. Pigou, The Economics of Welfare, 1920); the model's 40 versus 35 is the instance.

claims.text: The lesson is a model: straight lines, harm valued at $1 per loaf for illustration, no claim about any policy.
claims.source: Assumptions of Demo.tsx; stage chip 'Model: straight lines, invented numbers'.

recall.question: In the same bread model, each loaf puts $2 of smoke on neighbours. How many loaves match the true total cost?
recall.why: (100 - q) / 10 = (q + 20) / 10 + 2 gives 100 - q = q + 40, so q = 30, five fewer loaves for each extra dollar of harm.
